result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.random_edge_walk()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Perform a random walk and track the edges traversed. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L23469-L23640){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.random_edge_walk( start, steps, mode="out", stuck="return", seed=None, attr_name=None, return_list=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Like `random_walk()`, but operates on edges instead of nodes. Can return the sequence of edges as a list, or store the traversal order as an edge attribute for visualization. Time complexity: `O(steps)`, plus `O(degree)` per step for edge lookup. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [start]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Starting node (integer ID or string label). [steps]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of steps to take in the walk. [mode]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["out"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Direction to follow edges: (1) `"out"` to follow outgoing edges, (2) `"in"` to follow incoming edges, and (3) `"all"` to ignore edge direction. [stuck]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["return"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : What to do if the walk gets stuck. Use `"return"` to return the partial walk and use `"error"` to raise an error. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Random seed for reproducibility. If `None`, uses system entropy. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the edge attribute to store traversal order. If `None`, uses `random_edge_walk_order`. Only used when `return_list=False`. [return_list]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, return list of edge tuples. If `False`, store traversal order as edge attributes and return Graph for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[tuple[int, int, int]] | Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_list=True`: List of (edge_id, source_id, target_id) tuples. If `return_list=False`: Self for method chaining, with edge traversal order stored as edge attributes. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If start node not found, or invalid mode/stuck parameter. [RuntimeError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If walk gets stuck and `stuck="error"`. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Where `random_walk()` tracks the sequence of nodes visited, this variant records the sequence of edges *traversed*, which is the natural view for edge-centric analyses. Counting how many times each edge appears across a long walk gives a Monte Carlo estimate of the stationary edge-transition probability, which turns into an edge-importance ranking, a graph-sketching primitive, or a sanity check against analytic transition matrices. Because it returns `self` when `return_list=False` and stores per-walk attributes under a customizable name, several walks can be chained side by side under different attribute labels and later compared without recomputation. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Walking a triangle for 5 steps returns 5 traversed edges, each as an `(edge_id, source_id, target_id)` tuple: ::: {#b8445c57 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_edge(source="A", target="B") .add_edge(source="B", target="C") .add_edge(source="C", target="A") ) edges = graph.random_edge_walk("A", steps=5, seed=23, return_list=True) # Returns 5 edges traversed during the walk len(edges) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 5 ``` ::: ::: Rather than returning the list, the traversal order can be stashed on each edge as an attribute, which is handy for later analysis or visualization: ::: {#575f06f6 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.random_edge_walk("A", steps=100, seed=23) # Access traversal order from edge attributes orders = graph.get_edge_attrs_by_id("random_edge_walk_order") # Every edge was crossed at least once during 100 steps on a 3-edge triangle len(orders) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: Because it returns `self` when `return_list=False`, multiple walks can be chained together under different attribute names for comparison: ::: {#a931d04b .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_cycle_graph(6) .random_edge_walk(1, steps=50, seed=23, attr_name="walk1") .random_edge_walk(1, steps=50, seed=123, attr_name="walk2") ) walk1_orders = graph.get_edge_attrs_by_id("walk1") walk2_orders = graph.get_edge_attrs_by_id("walk2") # Edges visited by both walks common_edges = set(walk1_orders.keys()) & set(walk2_orders.keys()) len(common_edges) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 6 ``` ::: ::: Counting how often each edge is crossed over many steps reveals which connections the walk relies on most: ::: {#58714110 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} from collections import Counter graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_edge(source="A", target="B") .add_edge(source="B", target="C") .add_edge(source="C", target="A") ) edges = graph.random_edge_walk(start="A", steps=1000, seed=23, return_list=True) edge_counts = Counter((src_id, tgt_id) for _, src_id, tgt_id in edges) # Returns the most frequently crossed edges edge_counts.most_common(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` [((1, 2), 334), ((2, 3), 333), ((3, 1), 333)] ``` ::: :::
